summary.text: For squarefree \(n\), the identity \(\sum_{k=1}^n\gcd(k,n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\,\varphi(n/d)\) and multiplicativity give \(\prod_{p\mid n}(2p-1)\). Taking \(n=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341=23492890653051\) yields this product as \(26n-1\), so the relevant gcd is \(n\) although \(n\) is composite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(k,n),
\qquad
a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,1+S(n))}.
\]
We will exhibit a positive composite integer \(n\) for which \(a(n)=1\).

First we derive the form of \(S(n)\) that will make the counterexample easy to evaluate. Let \(\varphi\) denote Euler's totient function. For every positive integer \(n\), group the integers \(k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) according to the value
\(d=\gcd(k,n)\). Such a value \(d\) is necessarily a divisor of \(n\). For a fixed divisor \(d\mid n\), writing \(k=dj\) gives
\[
\gcd(k,n)=d
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
1\leq j\leq n/d\ \text{ and }\ \gcd(j,n/d)=1.
\]
There are exactly \(\varphi(n/d)\) such values of \(j\). Every corresponding term in the gcd-sum has value \(d\). Consequently
\[
S(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\,\varphi(n/d). \tag{1}
\]

This formula also shows that \(S\) is multiplicative. Indeed, suppose \(m\) and \(n\) are coprime. Every divisor of \(mn\) is uniquely of the form \(ab\), where \(a\mid m\) and \(b\mid n\). Moreover, \(m/a\) and \(n/b\) are coprime, so multiplicativity of Euler's totient gives
\[
\varphi\left(\frac{mn}{ab}\right)
=
\varphi\left(\frac ma\right)\varphi\left(\frac nb\right).
\]
Substituting this divisor parametrization into (1), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(mn)
&=\sum_{a\mid m}\sum_{b\mid n}
 ab\,\varphi(m/a)\varphi(n/b)\\
&=\left(\sum_{a\mid m}a\varphi(m/a)\right)
  \left(\sum_{b\mid n}b\varphi(n/b)\right)\\
&=S(m)S(n). \tag{2}
\end{aligned}
\]
For a prime \(p\), the only divisors are \(1\) and \(p\), so (1) gives
\[
S(p)=\varphi(p)+p\varphi(1)=(p-1)+p=2p-1. \tag{3}
\]
It follows from (2) and (3) that if \(n=p_1\cdots p_r\) is a product of distinct primes, then
\[
S(n)=\prod_{i=1}^r(2p_i-1). \tag{4}
\]

We now take the five numbers
\[
3,\quad 37,\quad 43,\quad 42307,\quad 116341.
\]
They are distinct primes. For completeness, here are elementary checks of the two nontrivial primality assertions, as well as the small auxiliary assertions used in those checks.

We use the following standard order criterion. Suppose \(N>1\), the complete prime factorization of \(N-1\) is known, and there is an integer \(b\) such that
\[
b^{N-1}\equiv1\pmod N
\]
and, for every prime \(q\mid N-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(b^{(N-1)/q}-1,N\bigr)=1. \tag{5}
\]
Then \(N\) is prime. To see this, let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(N\). The first congruence says that the multiplicative order of \(b\) modulo \(r\) divides \(N-1\). Condition (5) says that this order does not divide \((N-1)/q\) for any prime \(q\mid N-1\). Thus the order contains the full power of every prime occurring in \(N-1\), and hence is exactly \(N-1\). Since an element of \((\mathbb Z/r\mathbb Z)^\times\) has order dividing \(r-1\), we have \(N-1\mid r-1\), and therefore \(r\geq N\). But \(r\mid N\), so \(r\leq N\). Hence \(r=N\), proving that \(N\) itself is prime.

For \(N=42307\), we have
\[
N-1=42306=2\cdot3\cdot11\cdot641.
\]
The number \(641\) is prime: since \(25^2<641<26^2\), a composite \(641\) would have a prime divisor among \(2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23\). Its remainders modulo those primes, in that order, are
\[
1,2,1,4,3,4,12,14,20,
\]
all nonzero. The other factors \(2,3,11\) are plainly prime. With base \(b=3\), modular exponentiation gives
\[
3^{42306}\equiv1\pmod{42307},
\]
and the powers associated to the distinct prime divisors of \(42306\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q & 3^{42306/q}\bmod 42307 &
\gcd(3^{42306/q}-1,42307)\\ \hline
2&42306&1\\
3&36715&1\\
11&17937&1\\
641&10961&1.
\end{array}
\]
The gcd entries follow directly by the Euclidean algorithm applied to one less than each displayed residue and \(42307\). Thus the order criterion proves that \(42307\) is prime.

For \(N=116341\), the factorization is
\[
N-1=116340=2^2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot277.
\]
The number \(277\) is prime: because \(16^2<277<17^2\), it is enough to test the possible prime divisors \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), and the corresponding remainders are
\[
1,1,2,4,2,4.
\]
With base \(b=14\), modular exponentiation gives
\[
14^{116340}\equiv1\pmod{116341},
\]
and
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q & 14^{116340/q}\bmod 116341 &
\gcd(14^{116340/q}-1,116341)\\ \hline
2&116340&1\\
3&50801&1\\
5&81650&1\\
7&10889&1\\
277&35125&1.
\end{array}
\]
Again the last column is obtained by the Euclidean algorithm. The order criterion therefore proves that \(116341\) is prime.

For the remaining factors, ordinary trial division suffices. A composite number below \(49\) has a prime divisor at most \(7\). Neither \(37\) nor \(43\) is divisible by \(2,3,5\): their respective remainder lists are
\[
37:\ (1,1,2),
\qquad
43:\ (1,1,3).
\]
Thus both are prime, and \(3\) is prime as well. Since all five displayed primes are distinct, they are pairwise coprime, so formula (4) applies to their product.

Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
n
&=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341\\
&=23492890653051.
\end{aligned}
\]
The successive products of the prime factors are
\[
3,\quad111,\quad4773,\quad201931311,\quad23492890653051,
\]
which also records a direct check of the displayed value of \(n\). Formula (4) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(n)
&=(2\cdot3-1)(2\cdot37-1)(2\cdot43-1)
  (2\cdot42307-1)(2\cdot116341-1)\\
&=5\cdot73\cdot85\cdot84613\cdot232681.
\end{aligned}
\]
For clarity, the successive products on the last line are
\[
5,\quad365,\quad31025,\quad2625118325,\quad610815156979325.
\]
Hence
\[
S(n)=610815156979325.
\]
The crucial numerical identity is
\[
1+S(n)
=610815156979326
=26\cdot23492890653051
=26n. \tag{6}
\]
Thus \(n\mid 1+S(n)\). It follows that
\[
\gcd(n,1+S(n))=n,
\]
and, since \(n>0\),
\[
a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,1+S(n))}=\frac nn=1. \tag{7}
\]

On the other hand, \(n\) is certainly not \(1\), and it is not prime: for example,
\[
n=3\cdot7830963551017,
\]
with both factors strictly between \(1\) and \(n\). Therefore, at the positive composite integer
\[
\boxed{n=23492890653051},
\]
the assertion \(a(n)=1\) is true, while the assertion “\(n=1\) or \(n\) is prime” is false. This contradicts the proposed equivalence and disproves the conjecture.
